title: Chalk Talk: Brendan Sorsby Dispute Moves from NCAA Eligibility Challenge to Potential ...
description:
From NCAA Eligibility Dispute to Potential NFL Labor Fight Sorsby was originally declared ineligible by the NCAA following an investigation into sports wagering activity that reportedly involved more than 9,000 bets totaling approximately $90,000.
Although Sorsby did not participate in the games at issue, the NCAA nevertheless imposed a season-long suspension for the 2026 football season.
Rather than continue pursuing the injunction, Sorsby announced that he intended to seek entry into the NFL Supplemental Draft.
Sorsby submitted his application for the NFL Supplemental Draft three business days before the league's June 22, 2026 deadline.
Why the Brendan Sorsby Case Matters for NCAA Eligibility and the NFL Supplemental Draft The Sorsby matter illustrates how modern athlete disputes increasingly extend beyond traditional NCAA eligibility questions and into broader issues involving NIL arrangements, professional league access, and labor law.
text:
What began as an NCAA eligibility dispute involving former Texas Tech quarterback Brendan Sorsby may now be evolving into a broader legal battle involving professional football and the NFL's Supplemental Draft process.

From NCAA Eligibility Dispute to Potential NFL Labor Fight

Sorsby was originally declared ineligible by the NCAA following an investigation into sports wagering activity that reportedly involved more than 9,000 bets totaling approximately $90,000. According to court filings, the NCAA alleged that more than 40 of those wagers involved teams on which Sorsby was rostered while playing college football. Although Sorsby did not participate in the games at issue, the NCAA nevertheless imposed a season-long suspension for the 2026 football season.

In response, Sorsby filed suit in Texas state court seeking injunctive relief. In June 2026, the court granted a temporary injunction that allowed him to participate during the 2026 season after serving a two-game suspension, with the merits of the dispute to be addressed at a later trial following the football season.

The ruling was met with immediate legal pushback from the NCAA and the Big 12 Conference. The Big 12 Conference reportedly sought to enforce conference bylaws by imposing sanctions against Texas Tech, while the NCAA sought an accelerated trial before the start of the season.

Before those issues could be litigated further, however, Sorsby changed course.

Rather than continue pursuing the injunction, Sorsby announced that he intended to seek entry into the NFL Supplemental Draft. Because eligibility for the Supplemental Draft required him to be ineligible for the 2026 college football season, Sorsby voluntarily withdrew his lawsuit, thereby reinstating the NCAA's original determination that he was ineligible. Texas Tech publicly accepted the decision and indicated that it would not pursue repayment of NIL compensation previously provided to Sorsby.

The dispute then shifted from college athletics to professional football.

Sorsby submitted his application for the NFL Supplemental Draft three business days before the league's June 22, 2026 deadline. On June 23, however, the NFL announced that it had rejected the application and that no Supplemental Draft would be conducted in 2026. The NFL expressed concerns over the timing of Sorsby's application and the lack of information and documentation provided with respect to issues "too closely tied to the League's core integrity interests."

Potential Legal Issues Under the NFL Collective Bargaining Agreement

The NFL's decision has generated a new set of legal questions. Sorsby's attorney has publicly argued that the league's refusal to admit Sorsby into the Supplemental Draft violates the NFL's collective bargaining agreement and applicable law. Although no lawsuit has yet been filed, public statements from Sorsby's legal team indicate that legal action is under consideration.

Any challenge would likely present issues distinct from those raised in the NCAA litigation. A dispute involving the Supplemental Draft could implicate collectively bargained league rules, labor law principles, and the discretion afforded to professional sports leagues when administering player-entry mechanisms. While Sorsby is not currently an NFL player, any litigation could raise questions regarding provisions negotiated between the NFL and the NFLPA governing player-entry procedures and eligibility for the Supplemental Draft.

Why the Brendan Sorsby Case Matters for NCAA Eligibility and the NFL Supplemental Draft

The Sorsby matter illustrates how modern athlete disputes increasingly extend beyond traditional NCAA eligibility questions and into broader issues involving NIL arrangements, professional league access, and labor law. The case is also notable because Sorsby may find himself challenging the actions of a professional league he hopes to join in the future—an unusual dynamic that could create strategic considerations for both sides. Moreover, the dispute presents an interesting question regarding the role of collectively bargained rules in professional sports. Although it remains unclear whether the NFLPA would take a position on the matter, any litigation could require courts to examine provisions of the NFL-NFLPA Collective Bargaining Agreement governing player-entry procedures and the administration of the Supplemental Draft.

Unlike the NCAA litigation, which centered on the NCAA's eligibility rules, any challenge to the NFL's decision could test the extent to which a prospective player may invoke rights arising under a collectively bargained agreement before ever becoming a member of the bargaining unit. That threshold issue alone could make the case significant beyond the immediate dispute over Sorsby's draft eligibility.

Finally, the practical consequences for Sorsby are significant. By withdrawing his NCAA lawsuit, Sorsby forfeited the opportunity to continue pursuing participation during the 2026 college football season. If he is ultimately unable to gain entry into the Supplemental Draft and no alternative path emerges through litigation or negotiation, he may be forced to remain sidelined from competitive football until the 2027 NFL Draft cycle. More broadly, the dispute serves as a reminder that sports governing bodies remain committed to protecting the integrity of competition through the vigorous enforcement of gambling rules.

text:
After undergoing left foot surgery in January, Cowboys cornerback DaRon Bland was limited during spring workouts. Now, four weeks from training camp, Bland says his foot has healed, Jon Machota of The Athletic reports. He is expected to be a full participant when the Cowboys begin camp on July 29.

Last season was the second straight injury-shortened year for Bland, whose problems began when he fractured his left foot in 2024. That injury held Bland to seven games and zero interceptions, but it did not stop the Cowboys from handing him a four-year, $92MM extension a few days before last season opened.

Dallas’ defense went on to endure immense struggles in 2025, and Bland’s ongoing health troubles contributed to the unit’s issues. Injuries to both feet led to a 12-game campaign for Bland, who pulled in one INT and yielded a 103.3 passer rating on 77 targets.

While Bland’s previous two seasons were disappointing, he is not far removed from establishing himself as an elite ball hawk. During a 17-game rookie year in 2022, Bland picked off five passes and held QBs to an 82.2 rating on 63 targets. Bland’s stock continued to rise over another full season in 2023, in which he nabbed a league-high nine INTs and gave up a paltry 60.8 rating on 84 targets. He earned first-team All-Pro and Pro Bowl honors for his efforts.
